ten-frame.count-to-10.make-n.animals: Counting to ten is one of the very first big milestones in a child's math journey, and a ten-frame makes it wonderfully clear. In this free activity, children place friendly animal counters into a ten-frame and count from 0 to 10, building each number one square at a time.

Because the ten-frame always has ten spaces, children quickly start to see numbers in relation to ten — they notice that seven is "three away from full," or that five fills exactly half the frame. This visual sense of quantity is far more powerful than memorising a counting song, and it sets the stage for adding and subtracting later.

The activity is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.4, which connects counting to cardinality — understanding that the last number you count tells you how many there are in all. There is no timer and no score; children simply count, check, and try again as often as they like.
ten-frame.count-to-20.make-n.fruits: Once children are comfortable counting to ten, the next step is to stretch their thinking to twenty. This free activity uses a double ten-frame and cheerful fruit counters so children can count from 0 to 20 while still seeing the all-important group of ten.

Seeing twenty as "one full ten and some more" is a quiet but crucial idea. It helps children count larger amounts without losing track, and it plants the seed for place value — the understanding that our whole number system is built around tens.

Aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.4, this activity extends cardinality past ten in a calm, hands-on way. Children place fruit into the frames, count the total, and get gentle feedback with no timer and no score.
ten-frame.how-many.0-10.animals: "How many do you see?" is a question young children answer dozens of times a day, and this free activity turns it into playful practice. Children look at animal counters arranged on a ten-frame and decide how many are there, for amounts from 0 to 10.

Because the ten-frame organises the counters neatly, many children begin to recognise quantities at a glance — a skill called subitising — instead of counting each one. That instant recognition is a sign that real number sense is taking hold.

The activity is aligned to Common Core K.CC.B.5: counting to answer "how many?" There is no timer and no score, so children can take all the time they need to look, count, and feel sure of their answer.
ten-frame.write-numeral.0-20.fruits: Connecting a quantity to the written numeral is a key early-writing-in-math skill, and this free activity makes the link clear. Children count fruit on a double ten-frame and then write the matching number from 0 to 20.

Moving from "I can see fifteen pieces of fruit" to "I can write the numeral 15" ties together two ways of representing the same idea. The ten-frame keeps the quantity visible and organised, so the number a child writes always has a concrete picture behind it.

Aligned to Common Core K.CC.A.3 — representing a number of objects with a written numeral — the activity gives gentle, immediate feedback with no timer and no score, so writing numbers stays a relaxed, confidence-building experience.
ten-frame.teen-numbers.make-n: The teen numbers, eleven through nineteen, trip up a lot of young learners, because their names do not always match how they are written. This free activity uses a double ten-frame to show every teen number as exactly what it is: one full ten and some extra ones.

When a child builds fourteen as a complete ten plus four more, the structure of the number becomes obvious. This "ten and some ones" view is the single most important idea for understanding place value, and it makes later addition and subtraction far easier.

Aligned to Common Core K.NBT.A.1, the activity lets children build each teen number at their own pace, with warm feedback and no timer or score. It is a small activity that quietly unlocks a very big idea.
